newsitem.title: CHINA: Foreign affairs high on China premier's agenda.
newsitem.headline: Foreign affairs high on China premier's agenda.

text.p: Li Peng ended his last session of parliament as China's premier on a diplomatic note on Friday, making clear that Beijing sought better ties with both Moscow and Washington but denying it ever financed the U.S. Democrats.

A carefully choreographed series of questions underlined China's growing attention to its role on the international stage, with Li focusing on foreign affairs at his last scheduled news conference before he steps down next year, diplomats said.

A solution was near to the squabble between Pyongyang and Seoul over the most senior North Korean official to defect to the South, Li told a news conference after the annual session of the National People's Congress, or parliament, closed.
Li told Britain that it should mind its own business after Hong Kong reverts to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30 following 150 years of British colonial government.
All except one of the questions, which officials had arranged for foreign and Chinese journalists to field at Li's news conference, involved international relations.

Li waved aside allegations that Beijing had tried to fund politicians in the United States and said China would roll out the red carpet for U.S. Vice President Al Gore when he visits China later this month.

China opposes other countries intervening in its internal affairs and would not use any means to interfere with or influence any other country's domestic affairs, Li said when asked to comment on allegations that China funded the U.S. Democrats.
Beijing would take good care of Gore when he visited China March 24-28. Gore will "receive very good treatment", Li said.
However, Li counteracted the rapid warming in Sino-U.S. ties -- due to culminate in an exchange of presidential visits later this year -- by stressing relations with Russia.
President Jiang Zemin is to visit Russia in April to sign an agreement to cut troops along China's border with Russia and three Central Asian states -- Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan, Li said.
"It will be conducive to peace and friendly neighbourly relations along the borders," Li said.

Asked about progress in negotiations on the fate of North Korean defector Hwang Jang-yop, sheltering in Seoul's Beijing consulate since February 12, Li said: "I can tell you conditions are nearly ripe for solving this problem."
Hwang has said he wants to go to South Korea and diplomats have said that he would likely be allowed to leave for a third country first and then travel to Seoul.
Premier Li gave little hint as to how the month-long standoff would end, although he said stability on the tense Korean peninsula was a key consideration.
China and North Korea fought side by side in the 1950-53 Korean War but Beijing has been drawn closer to Seoul as it pushes ahead with rapid development under market-style economic reforms.
On the recovery of Hong Kong -- hailed by China as one of the highlights of 1997 -- Li pledged that Beijing would not intervene after the territory reverts to Chinese rule.
The Hong Kong Special Administrative Region would be highly autonomous, he said, repeating China's favourite adage that "Hong Kong people will rule Hong Kong".
He said it would be unrealistic for Hong Kong's outgoing colonial master, Britain, to monitor the territory after July 1 because it would then be purely China's internal affair.
